text: We will also focus on digital inclusion in our community centres.

speaker: The Minister for Foreign Affairs (Dr Vivian Balakrishnan)
text: Members have heard about the Silver Infocomm Initiative, and this is a way.

speaker: The Minister for Foreign Affairs (Dr Vivian Balakrishnan)
text: Even when people do not own any smart phones, cannot use technology and we have to handhold, train, provide so that everyone can ride on this.

speaker: The Minister for Foreign Affairs (Dr Vivian Balakrishnan)
text: What is our unique selling point or competitive advantage?

speaker: The Minister for Foreign Affairs (Dr Vivian Balakrishnan)
text: I believe we are approaching this from a position of strength.

speaker: The Minister for Foreign Affairs (Dr Vivian Balakrishnan)
text: We continue to offer one of the best digital infrastructures in the world.

speaker: The Minister for Foreign Affairs (Dr Vivian Balakrishnan)
text: Second, our people are well-educated, well-trained and tech-savvy.

speaker: The Minister for Foreign Affairs (Dr Vivian Balakrishnan)
text: Third, we have only a single layer of Government.

speaker: The Minister for Foreign Affairs (Dr Vivian Balakrishnan)
text: And we have a Prime Minister who can code, a Prime Minister who certainly gets it, who is a mystery customer on many Government websites.

speaker: The Minister for Foreign Affairs (Dr Vivian Balakrishnan)
text: If it is a complaint, it is usually, especially a smart complaint, it is almost always the Prime Minister.

speaker: The Minister for Foreign Affairs (Dr Vivian Balakrishnan)
text: The key here is not just tech innovation but policy innovation and the spirit of internal disruption and the willingness to rewrite regulations, absorb ideas.

speaker: The Minister for Foreign Affairs (Dr Vivian Balakrishnan)
text: Another thing in which we want to be different is to feed our own start-ups by buying their services; and to be a test bed for novel solutions, for urban solutions and, especially, including in areas like fintech, transport, healthcare, homecare and social services.

speaker: The Minister for Foreign Affairs (Dr Vivian Balakrishnan)
text: To conclude, we need to urgently build skills and capabilities in our people and enterprises.

speaker: The Minister for Foreign Affairs (Dr Vivian Balakrishnan)
text: We need to ensure pole position, with the best infrastructure in the world, we need to be prepared to fundamentally disrupt the way the Government provides services.

speaker: The Minister for Foreign Affairs (Dr Vivian Balakrishnan)
text: We need to forge new partnerships with the private sector, we need to make sure our start-ups, especially, have access to technology and opportunities, and we need to be open to the global flow of talent and ideas.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: Generally, though, there is inverse correlation between development and TFR.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: The countries with the highest TFR now are the sub-Saharan African countries, while the developed countries are at the low end of the spectrum.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: Anecdotally, I understand that the incentives given to encourage marriage and parenthood have been helpful.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: In speaking to young parents, affordable and convenient childcare is high on the priority list of necessities as it is becoming more common for families to have working parents and grandparents.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: The most important generation now in this area is probably the millennials, that is, those born in the 1980s and early 1990s, as they would be in the prime years for marriage and parenting.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: What are the attitudes of our millennials towards marriage and parenthood?

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: Is there anything more we can do to support young Singaporeans in achieving marriage and parenthood aspirations, a club I recently joined myself?

speaker: Assoc Prof Fatimah Lateef
text: It is a process that involves the interaction and integration between the new immigrants and the receiving community or society.

speaker: Assoc Prof Fatimah Lateef
text: This can be done at the individual or collective level.

speaker: Assoc Prof Fatimah Lateef
text: The policies of a nation represent the litmus test for integration and citizenship approval.

speaker: Assoc Prof Fatimah Lateef
text: Our guidelines and policies must acknowledge our diversity and uphold unity, recognise the importance of local content and have a realistic framework, both at the national and community levels.

speaker: Assoc Prof Fatimah Lateef
text: New citizens can, indeed, have positive contributions towards nation building and social integration.

speaker: Assoc Prof Fatimah Lateef
text: Will our current appointment model and processes be reviewed and tweaked, in particular, to have a greater community involvement component?

speaker: Assoc Prof Fatimah Lateef
text: This may include, firstly, performance of voluntary and community services which helps in immersion and integration with the community one lives in; and secondly, getting active and senior grassroots as well as community leaders to nominate or become assenters for the potential new citizens.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: However, I am concerned about the possibility of one-sidedness in the political education exposure that new citizens receive.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: In the SCJ HOME for new citizens guide, there are brief overviews of our political system explaining the role of elections, Parliament and so on.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: However, two matters stand out that are of concern.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: In the course of the SCJ process, such as citizenship ceremonies, for example, they are exposed to and may get to meet People's Action Party politicians but not politicians from other parties.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: One older new citizen who is highly educated in credential, told me that he supported more balance and competition in our system but was afraid that if he voted for the Workers' Party, the Government would find out and take away his citizenship.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: We spent 10 minutes trying to explain the process by which votes are kept secret.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: At the end of the 10 minutes, I am not sure if we had convinced him.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: I could not find this being treated at all in the HOME for new citizens guidebook.

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak (Sembawang)
text: It has become more pressing than ever, now that we are tackling the existing issues that are putting Singaporeans off raising children.

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak (Sembawang)
text: Citing high costs of living and personal ambitions, there are more mothers who wish that they are able to continue their careers with minimal disruption.

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak (Sembawang)
text: More women are returning to the workforce and, with the higher retirement age, even grandparents are giving up babysitting duties for jobs.

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak (Sembawang)
text: All this spells good for our labour force, but it gives rise to the pressing need to build up our caregiving support system for infants and young children, allowing young parents to have a safe haven to deposit their children while they focus on bringing the bread home.

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak (Sembawang)
text: The Government has done a lot to make childcare services more accessible for all parents.

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak (Sembawang)
text: Lack of vacancies in some of the more populated estates is a common grouse.

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak (Sembawang)
text: Moreover, lately, some childcare centres have been in the headlines for improper handling of their young charges, and this can create a misconception about the state of childcare services in Singapore.

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak (Sembawang)
text: On the other hand, some parents prefer to keep their young children at home for a variety of reasons.

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak (Sembawang)
text: Some do this because there is no vacancy in centres within a convenient location.

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak (Sembawang)
text: Others do it because it is almost impossible to coordinate their work schedule with the centre's hours.

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak (Sembawang)
text: Perhaps, the child has underlying conditions that make it difficult for him or her to spend long hours outside the home with a large group of children.

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak (Sembawang)
text: We cannot dismiss the concerns of this group of parents.

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak (Sembawang)
text: How can we help them find adequately-trained caregivers to care for the child in the comfort of a home?

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak (Sembawang)
text: The Government has already implemented a slew of measures to encourage flexible working hours that are meant for catering to a family-friendly model.

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak (Sembawang)
text: While the public sector may have dutifully abided by these measures, not all private companies will follow suit.

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak (Sembawang)
text: In fact, some consider it a hassle and are unable to cope with what they perceive as a manpower shortage.

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak (Sembawang)
text: In fact, flexible work hours do not necessarily have anything to do with reducing working hours.

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak (Sembawang)
text: It is to do with changing our work habits to improve productivity and work-life balance.

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak (Sembawang)
text: And while we are on the subject of working hours, some childcare centres only operate the same hours as a typical office employee's working hours.

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak (Sembawang)
text: Many employees are unable to knock off on the dot, and even so, they cannot fully teleport themselves to the centre to pick up their child on time.

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak
text: How can we provide more help for these parents to cope with these challenges?

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling
text: Perhaps, arising from all this baby goodness, I had a baby myself and attended several 100-day baby showers with my loved one on my hip.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling
text: At 100 days old, the babies were just cherubic enough to undergo a baby massage, participate in baby gym and be dressed in bunny outfits.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling
text: The mummies had organised the baby showers all by themselves, sometimes involving a hundred babies at one go.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling
text: They set up Facebook groups, discussed via whatsapp, sometimes in the middle of the night as they fed their babies and looked to one another for mutual support.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling
text: It was a time of bliss, of sisterhood and camaraderie.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling
text: But as the maternity leave started coming to an end, the worries started coming in. "Grandma's too far away in Ang Mo Kio (or Hougang, or Serangoon) and she would rather get together with her friends than take care of baby", they say. "My maternity leave is for four months and I need to go back to work urgently in this economic climate.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling
text: There is no available infantcare spot in Punggol, given the large number of infants here.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling
text: What do I do?", "MOE is starting up some kindergartens in Punggol but I work and need a childcare spot, not kindergarten.", "Infantcare or childcare closes at 7.00 pm and I am fined for every 15 minutes I am late picking up my child.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling
text: So, I am late all the time and my child is starving by the time I get to her.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling
text: I feel like a bad mum all the time.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling
text: What do I do?" Of stress, uncertainty and conflict.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling
text: Of solutions available to young parents but not quite solving the problem.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling
text: Of gaps between options that leave young parents in a bind.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling
text: Can we start looking at policies in a continuous spectrum to help young parents, where solutions are available every step of the way mirroring the decisions they have to make as baby grows up?

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling
text: Can infantcare progression to childcare be seamless and not cause parents to fret, queuing for a spot every few years?

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling
text: Can a community of caregivers be trained to help young parents pick up their child or provide a hot meal when they are caught up?

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling
text: It would be a loss to their joy as a family if inconveniences and uncertainty stop them from having children.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling
text: It would also be a loss to the state.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling
text: Can we pull the Government machinery together to offer seamless solutions for our young families?

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling
text: For then, we can pop the confetti and celebrate, and bring on the baby showers.

speaker: The Chairman
text: Ms Tin Pei Ling, you have two cuts.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: During the COS last year, I spoke of offering alternative childcare options other than care centres and familial support, which not everyone has.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: I also suggested taping on experienced community nannies and how the Government can help to better match supply and demand.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: Building on what I spoke about last year, I would like to ask if the NPTD had studied possible alternative childcare options and, if so, what were the findings?

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: Does the Government have plans to implement some of the alternatives found to be viable?

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: Parents naturally want the best for our children.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: Some of the key considerations that parents have when deciding on childcare are safety and curriculum quality.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: Making sure that a child is properly cared for and engaged not only ensures the child's well-being, it also strengthens our country's workforce and prepares future generations to be competitive in the future global economy.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: Therefore, if childcare alternatives, such as community nannies, are to be implemented, how does the Government intend to ensure that children in these alternative care settings will also receive quality and safe care, such that these alternatives become viable options for parents who need but cannot secure centre-based childcare services?

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: A key factor driving couples' decision on when to have children is when they can secure their own homes.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: Having a child is a life-changing decision and a lifetime commitment.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: Naturally, couples want to make sure that they achieve a certain security so that they can better focus on raising the child.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: The Government continues to supply new flats and, eventually, supply will meet demand.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: But there is always a lag of three to four years because of the time needed to build the flats after the ballot.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: With couples marrying later in life, each day that passes by in waiting is a precious opportunity wasted to have a child.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: In Singapore, where our TFR is far from ideal, this is no doubt a big challenge that we must solve, and it can be solved.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: At my recent MPS, I met a couple in their late 30s.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: They found each other late in life and so got married late.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: But the biological clock is frantically ticking away.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: They balloted for a flat twice but were unsuccessful.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: They cannot live in either of their parents' place due to serious space constraints and other sensitive considerations.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: For couples like them, who are sincere and anxious to have children soon, should we not help them?

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: Lest couples become disincentivised to continue balloting for a flat and settle for a PPHS rental unit instead, the Government could build in a condition stating that they can have the unit for a year, renewable for another year maximum, and they must book a flat within this period.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: If they successfully book one within the period, they can continue to live in the flat till their own flat is ready.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: The joy of having a child cannot be measured by any tangible means and the decision to have a child must come from the heart.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: The Government cannot decide for couples, but the Government can certainly help by removing barriers and catalysing the making of families.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: I have made that choice and I can honestly say that my two children are an amazing blessing as they bring so much joy to myself and my wife.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: It is also true that having and raising a child does have its challenging moments, especially when they are very young.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: However, I believe that if we can enhance the experience of families with young children and infants, then this would not only give them much needed support, it could also encourage them to have more children.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Much has been done by the NPTD and MSF to provide support in infantcare, childcare and student care.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: My colleagues, Ms Sun Xueling and Ms Tin Pei Ling, have also raised some suggestions in this area.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: But I would like to focus on how perhaps more could also be done in the area of providing housing options for families with infants and young children.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: I believe this could be a win-win situation that will allow smaller family units to rent these flats, while ensuring that these flats do not remain empty and unused.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: I hope that NPTD can consider this suggestion.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: Work and the resultant time left for children is a critical factor in families' decision for children.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: Thus, transforming our workplaces and how we work can help to tackle Singapore's fertility issues.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: The technological revolution challenges us to explore new frontiers for flexible work arrangements (FWA).

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: We should and must now ride on the technological advances and make technology-enabled FWA more pervasive.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: For example, telecommuting is now more accessible through cloud services and video conferencing.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: Customer enquiries can be handled away from office.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: We can also develop more shared working spaces in community spaces and heartlands for caregivers to work away from the office.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: Our libraries and some community clubs already have them, but building a larger network of such spaces can even provide companies with more options to engage their employees.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: In the meantime, we can develop a marketplace for Government and Singapore companies to put up "gigs" or smaller jobs and projects that caregivers can do away from home.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: These gigs or micro jobs can be consulting projects, accounts, helping with customer service replies or even social services.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: A parent has six days of childcare leave until the child becomes seven years old when she only gets two days.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: Yet, the child's health and independence is a gradual one.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: This system allows parents to gradually transit in their caregiving until their child matures.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: It also helps families with more than one child.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: Currently, they get two days when their children are in Primary school.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: Yet, the needs of a lower Primary and an upper Primary child can be rather different.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: The most resistance, ultimately, to working flexibly is cultural.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: We must practise progressive senior leadership, building a nurturing environment of trust and mindset are critical in transforming our workplaces.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: This is why flexible work arrangements (FWAs) must be the way to go.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: My wife and I have three young children.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: I just want to share that in deciding to move from the second to the third child, to be honest, the flexible work arrangement my wife experienced was a significant factor for us to move from two to three.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Some employers think it simply means shorter working hours and more days off for the employee in question, and they lament the shortage of staff that this results in.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: In worst cases, they discriminate and refuse to hire people whom they think are prone to requiring FWAs.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: So, it is imperative that we transform employers' mindsets so that they are willing to embrace this style of working and incorporate it in their workplaces.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: I note that according to MOM's Conditions of Employment survey, the situation is improving.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: This is a positive indication, but we can do more to nudge the other about 30% to get on board, especially the local SMEs.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Under the Work-Life Grant, employers receive grants and reimbursements, and they may even engage consultants to help create and implement good work-life strategies for the company.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: However, companies must apply and, in the first place, if they have misconceptions about FWA, they would not be proactive about it.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Let them start slow, with one FWA and perhaps two Singaporean employees utilising FWA to allow them to benefit from the grants.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Taking the first step is always the hardest.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: If the step is too high, many people will not even have the ability to clear it.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: May the two lovely girls grow in health and be full of the same fighting spirit that their father has.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: There is one instinct that is more powerful than even that of survival, and it is the instinct that comes with parenthood.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: From my own limited experience with my wife, parenthood sometimes brings out the superhuman in you.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: Suddenly, you find yourself faster running after the kids, stronger carrying both squirming boys at once, braver standing up to the pesky cockroach in the kitchen and perhaps somewhat wiser as well.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: But it will be untruthful of me to just paint parenthood and family life as just being a bed of roses.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: There are, definitely, downtimes when you feel insufficient, deficient even, unworthy.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: Having kids sometimes frustrates your plans, changes your lifestyle, cramps your style, messes up your hair, ruffles your feathers.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: But for the vast majority of parents, watching your little ones sleep peacefully, grow up healthily and in wisdom, there can be no greater reward for those sacrifices.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: Yet, in spite of the many joys of parenthood, the Prime Minister said at the recent Camp Sequoia dialogue that babies are one of the many issues that keeps him awake at night.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: Not that he is kept awake by bawling babies in the next room but by the general lack of babies in Singapore.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: In reality, it should be an issue that all Singaporeans should be worrying about as well.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: But this is not for the lack of incentives, as we have heard from many speakers before – more infant care centres, compulsory paternity leave, flexi-work arrangements, baby bonus and housing incentives.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: Short of going to the extreme, as the town of Overtornea, Sweden, is considering − paid time off once a week for municipal workers to pro-create − we cannot possibly be pumping endless cash and other incentives.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: What we lack today is no longer the how, but the why.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: We have assumed for a long time that cost is one of the prime reasons why birth rates are low, but we have addressed these concerns with a very generous package.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: I have argued in previous Budgets why we cannot reach a stage where we literally get paid to start families.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: That runs counter to the idea of family in the first place.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: We can support but we cannot over incentivise.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: What Singapore needs today is for us to realise that family is a key cornerstone for stability in our lives.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: A mindset change that we accept that parents have a special responsibility and should be supported by the wider community.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: Employers to know that a flustered mother turning up half hour late for work after struggling through the rain to send her kids to childcare is not taking advantage.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: What can the Ministry do in working with families, community groups and religious organisations even, to play a larger part?

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: And when we call for more, can the village also play a bigger role?

speaker: The Senior Minister of State, Prime Minister's Office (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: Deputy Prime Minister Teo spoke about managing our strategic resources, and there are none more precious than our people.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State, Prime Minister's Office (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: At Strategy Group in PMO, we work closely with agencies to bring the Government together on our national priorities, including to achieve a sustainable population and to strengthen our Singapore Family.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State, Prime Minister's Office (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: Our key priority is to provide strong support for marriage and parenthood.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State, Prime Minister's Office (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: With current immigration rates, we are able to maintain the size of the citizen population in the prime working ages at about 2.1-2.2 million.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State, Prime Minister's Office (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: Members will agree that the composition of our population matters as much as size.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State, Prime Minister's Office (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: One useful indicator is the Old-Age Support Ratio (OASR) which refers to the number of working-age citizens for every citizen aged 65 years and above.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State, Prime Minister's Office (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: This is the decline with current immigration rate.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State, Prime Minister's Office (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: A diminishing OASR has serious implications, including on the economic vitality we hope future generations of Singaporeans can enjoy.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State, Prime Minister's Office (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: But this is not a challenge unique to Singapore.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State, Prime Minister's Office (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: Besides Japan and South Korea which are also ageing rapidly, China will see its OASR halved from 7.1 in 2015 to about 3.6 in 2030.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State, Prime Minister's Office (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: Our closest neighbour Malaysia and Thailand will similarly see sharp declines in their OASRs.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State, Prime Minister's Office (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: A recent article in The Economist suggested that these countries may, in time to come, need millions of immigrants to bring about a better population balance.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State, Prime Minister's Office (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: However, as Assoc Prof Fatimah Lateef alluded to, immigration is a sensitive matter that has to be carefully managed.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State, Prime Minister's Office (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: It is not, and must not, be a numbers game.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State, Prime Minister's Office (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: Besides achieving a better population balance, we must consider the ability of new citizens to assimilate into our Singaporean family, which is itself increasingly diverse in origin and outlook.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State, Prime Minister's Office (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: Because of this, we conduct regular reviews of our immigration framework.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State, Prime Minister's Office (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: All PR and citizenship applications are assessed carefully and holistically.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State, Prime Minister's Office (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: For example, we take into account various markers of social integration, including the applicant's family ties to Singaporeans, their family profile and length of residency in Singapore.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State, Prime Minister's Office (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: We also consider the applicant's economic contributions, qualifications, age and other relevant factors.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State, Prime Minister's Office (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: We encourage all who wish to join the Singapore family to engage with and participate actively in their local communities, but this should not be done purely as a means to obtain citizenship.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State, Prime Minister's Office (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: All new citizens participate in the Singapore Citizenship Journey (SCJ), which Mr Leon Perera talked about.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State, Prime Minister's Office (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: Mr Perera knows, as well as I do, that there are no restrictions as to which constituency new citizens can live in and which political parties they can associate with.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State, Prime Minister's Office (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: For all citizens, we leave the decision to individuals whether and which political parties they wish to learn more about.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State, Prime Minister's Office (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: If this is how new citizens feel they can integrate into Singapore society, they are free to do so.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State, Prime Minister's Office (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: In any case, keeping in mind the importance of integration, the Government kept the pace of immigration stable.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State, Prime Minister's Office (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: In 2016, 22,102 Singapore Citizenships and 31,050 Permanent Residencies were granted.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State, Prime Minister's Office (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: The vast majority of adult new citizens have lived in Singapore for five years or more prior to naturalisation, contributing to Singapore society in various ways.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State, Prime Minister's Office (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: Members will note that with this pace of immigration, we are just maintaining and not growing the citizen population in the prime working ages.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State, Prime Minister's Office (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: This is also why we place priority on making Singapore a Great Place for Families, where young Singaporeans feel confident that marriage and parenthood are achievable, enjoyable and celebrated.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State, Prime Minister's Office (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: This will be the main focus of my response to Members' cuts.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State, Prime Minister's Office (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: Last year, we had 23,873 citizen marriages, an increase from our Golden Jubilee Year.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State, Prime Minister's Office (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: Citizen births fell slightly to 33,161, even though I know some Members of the House have done your part.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State, Prime Minister's Office (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: However, this slightly lower figure is still slightly higher than the average in the past 10 years of about 32,000 babies.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State, Prime Minister's Office (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: Mr Vikram Nair asked about the attitudes of young Singaporeans who are approaching the peak marriage and parenthood ages.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State, Prime Minister's Office (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: He will be pleased to know that Singaporean millennials − those in their mid-teens to early 30s − still have strong aspirations to marry and start families.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State, Prime Minister's Office (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: According to our survey last year, 83% of single millennials want to get married.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State, Prime Minister's Office (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: Among married respondents, 92% want to have at least two children.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State, Prime Minister's Office (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: We have identified three key areas which will help Singaporean millennials turn these aspirations into reality.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State, Prime Minister's Office (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: These are: faster access to public housing; more affordable and quality pre-school services; and greater workplace and community support.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State, Prime Minister's Office (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: At this COS, we are announcing a package of enhancements that are a significant boost to family formation for Singaporean millennials.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State, Prime Minister's Office (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: Due in large part to the success of our public housing programme, many couples now aspire to own their own homes before they start a family.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State, Prime Minister's Office (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: For example, the Parenthood Priority Scheme (PPS) gives priority allocation of new flats to first-timer married couples who are already parents but the PPS also offers the same benefit to couples who are not yet parents but are expecting a child.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State, Prime Minister's Office (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: Over 80% of first-timers buy new rather than resale flats.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State, Prime Minister's Office (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: Today, the average waiting time for BTO completion is three to four years which Ms Tin Pei Ling noted.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State, Prime Minister's Office (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: If these couples need their own place urgently, the Parenthood Provisional Housing Scheme (PPHS) provides interim rental housing at below market rates.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State, Prime Minister's Office (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: Later in the debate, Minister Lawrence Wong will outline plans to provide some BTO flats with shorter waiting times.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State, Prime Minister's Office (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: We will also share plans to enhance the PPHS to help more couples who want to live on their own while waiting for their BTO flats, including improving their affordability, as Mr Darryl David had hoped.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State, Prime Minister's Office (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: For couples who do not wish to wait or prefer to live near their parents, a good option is resale flats which about 20% of all first-timers have bought.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State, Prime Minister's Office (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: At the Budget Speech last week, the Finance Minister announced enhancements to the CPF Housing Grant.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State, Prime Minister's Office (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: With shorter waiting times, more accessible PPHS flats and higher resale grants in place, more couples will be able to enjoy a place of their own faster.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State, Prime Minister's Office (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: But I urge couples not to delay planning as a result.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State, Prime Minister's Office (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: There are many worthy pursuits in life and, if marriage and parenthood are to feature at all, they have to be prioritised earlier rather than later.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State, Prime Minister's Office (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: As I have said before, please do not wait till it is too late.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State, Prime Minister's Office (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: It is an area in which we will strengthen support for parents − childcare and, particularly, in the care of infants.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State, Prime Minister's Office (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: Today, many infants up to 18 months old are cared for at home by family members.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State, Prime Minister's Office (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: This is usually the mother or grandparent, sometimes with support from a domestic helper.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State, Prime Minister's Office (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: However, as Dr Lim Wee Kiak noted, more women and grandparents are entering or remaining in the workforce.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State, Prime Minister's Office (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: This is a positive development which adds to the vibrancy and depth of experience in our economy.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State, Prime Minister's Office (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: But it also means a growing need for care of infants outside of homes.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State, Prime Minister's Office (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: Today, a relatively small proportion of infants, 8%, are enrolled in centre-based infant care, but the satisfaction levels of these parents are as high as those whose infants are cared for at home.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State, Prime Minister's Office (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: The Early Childhood Development Agency (ECDA) will meet the growing demand for centre-based infant care by increasing capacity to over 8,000 places in the next few years.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State, Prime Minister's Office (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: The increased capacity will provide for around one in five newborns.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State, Prime Minister's Office (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: While we ramp up capacity, we will, at the same time, maintain quality.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State, Prime Minister's Office (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: The new Early Childhood Development Centres Bill, which was passed earlier this week, will help ensure greater consistency and standards across the whole sector.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State, Prime Minister's Office (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: I wish to assure Dr Lim Wee Kiak that ECDA also recognises the importance of matching supply to demand and will seek improvements in this area.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State, Prime Minister's Office (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: Dr Lim Wee Kiak and Ms Tin Pei Ling have pointed out that some families still prefer their infants to be cared for at home and asked how we might strengthen support for home-based care.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State, Prime Minister's Office (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: It is, therefore, heartening that NTUC's SEED Institute, which has trained many of our early childhood educators, will now look at sharing their expertise to help train domestic helpers.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State, Prime Minister's Office (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: SEED has collaborated with healthcare professionals from KK Women's and Children's Hospital to pilot an infant care training course for domestic helpers employed by families with young infants.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State, Prime Minister's Office (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: The course will equip these domestic helpers with the basic know-how to care for and interact with infants, with a focus on safety and hygiene, which are the key concerns of parents.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State, Prime Minister's Office (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: It also includes a module to help both the employers and their helpers establish a common understanding of how the infant should be cared for.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State, Prime Minister's Office (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: SEED and KK Hospital plan to offer 100 training places through this pilot.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State, Prime Minister's Office (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: If the response is positive, the pilot could be scaled up.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State, Prime Minister's Office (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: Other caregivers, such as nannies, babysitters or even parents themselves who wish to receive caregiving training, can use their SkillsFuture credits to attend several infant and childcare courses already available in the market.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State, Prime Minister's Office (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: Besides housing and childcare, the third important area of focus is workplace support.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State, Prime Minister's Office (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: Millennials, both men and women, want to have meaningful careers and fulfilling family lives.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State, Prime Minister's Office (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: Indeed, both sets of aspirations are worthy of support.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State, Prime Minister's Office (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: I share Ms Sun Xueling's view that we should look at support from the lens of a young parent and plug the gaps so that the transitions at each stage of the parenthood journey can be more seamless, and young parents can manage both family and work successfully.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State, Prime Minister's Office (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: We have introduced a number of enhancements in recent years which are welcomed by parents.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State, Prime Minister's Office (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: Enhancements to shared parental leave and adoption leave will also come into effect in July.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State, Prime Minister's Office (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: Parents are happy to have more time to care for and bond with their infants, and fathers can also play a bigger role in raising their newborns, all while remaining in employment.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State, Prime Minister's Office (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: However, even with the latest enhancements, the return to regular work may still be tough for those without strong family support and who need centre-based infant care.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State, Prime Minister's Office (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: Today, both working parents, together, can enjoy 20 weeks of paid leave in the first year after their child is born, and two weeks of unpaid leave.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State, Prime Minister's Office (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: Even though infant care centres are able to take in babies from the time they are two months old, most parents feel more confident when their babies are about six months or 26 weeks old.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State, Prime Minister's Office (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: For such parents, there could be a caregiving gap of around four weeks.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State, Prime Minister's Office (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: We want to provide better workplace support for these parents, while balancing the need for businesses to adjust to the recent parental leave enhancements.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State, Prime Minister's Office (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: Therefore, the public sector will take the lead to pilot a scheme to close the potential caregiving gap.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State, Prime Minister's Office (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: This means that as long as one parent is working in the Public Service, the couple can have up to 26 weeks of leave, or six months, between them.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State, Prime Minister's Office (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: Members may ask if the additional leave can be paid rather than unpaid.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State, Prime Minister's Office (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: Our observation is that even with paid parental leave, some parents have not been utilising them in full.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State, Prime Minister's Office (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: Some do not need all the leave provided; others face pressures at work that prevent them from taking more parental leave.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State, Prime Minister's Office (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: Further paid leave does not benefit these parents.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State, Prime Minister's Office (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: Instead, parents want better assurance of workplace support, that they can take all their parental leave provisions if they need them.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State, Prime Minister's Office (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: This is why we have decided that the main objectives of the pilot in the Public Service are to test the general viability of longer parental leave and to require all supervisors to facilitate such leave.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State, Prime Minister's Office (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: Under this pilot, supervisors in the public sector, which includes Ministries and Statutory Boards, will no longer be able to say "maybe yes, maybe no".

speaker: The Senior Minister of State, Prime Minister's Office (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: Both male and female public officers are eligible to apply.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State, Prime Minister's Office (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: As long as they have been given reasonable notice, supervisors will have to accede to all applications for such parental leave and make the necessary work adjustments.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State, Prime Minister's Office (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: The public sector pilot will also be for a longer period of three years so that we can adequately test the impact of longer parental leave in a variety of work settings.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State, Prime Minister's Office (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: These experiences will be useful in assessing whether a nation-wide rollout is practicable in future.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State, Prime Minister's Office (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: But I would like to add a word of caution here.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State, Prime Minister's Office (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: We should not under-estimate the challenges of such a move.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State, Prime Minister's Office (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: As it is, some employers face great difficulty in accommodating staff with childcare needs.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State, Prime Minister's Office (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: Some parents also tell us of the pushback they experience from co-workers.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State, Prime Minister's Office (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: Extending parental leave can, unwittingly, be an added source of tension at the workplace.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State, Prime Minister's Office (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: Therefore, I hope Members will help to rally support for the pilot and give us suggestions on how we can improve its chances of success.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State, Prime Minister's Office (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: Needless to say, while we are piloting this measure in the public sector only, we hope some private sector companies will also join in to lead the way.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State, Prime Minister's Office (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: I should also add that parental leave provisions can only do so much.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State, Prime Minister's Office (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: As many Members have pointed out, what employees want, increasingly, is flexibility.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State, Prime Minister's Office (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: MOM has a useful way of thinking about flexible work arrangements (FWAs) − flexi-time, flexi-place and flexi-load.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State, Prime Minister's Office (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: The data shows that two in three employees worked in companies that provided at least one form of FWAs.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State, Prime Minister's Office (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: Anecdotally, however, as Mr Saktiandi Supaat has suggested, many employees do not feel the impact of such support.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State, Prime Minister's Office (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: In any case, our survey last year revealed that eight in 10 married respondents cited having FWAs as an important consideration when deciding which company to join.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State, Prime Minister's Office (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: So, it appears that companies still have some catching up to do.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State, Prime Minister's Office (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: More recently, the tripartite partners have published an advisory which guides companies through the process of introducing FWAs.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State, Prime Minister's Office (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: MOM is studying ways to encourage more companies to come on board and will share more details later in the year.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State, Prime Minister's Office (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: I agree with Mr Alex Yam that Government action alone cannot bring about a mindset change.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State, Prime Minister's Office (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: They say it takes a village to raise a child.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State, Prime Minister's Office (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: And, in Singapore, we want the entire kampong to chip in.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State, Prime Minister's Office (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: Take, for example, the Trivelis Babies group, a ground-up initiative by residents of Trivelis estate in Clementi.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State, Prime Minister's Office (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: The group started when a few young parents were looking for mutual support in their parenthood journeys, and has grown organically to about 150 members.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State, Prime Minister's Office (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: They dovetail nicely with the many 100-day showers Ms Sun Xueling has attended.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State, Prime Minister's Office (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: MOT will give more details at next week's debate.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: (In Mandarin):   Mdm Chairman, we are committed to "Making Singapore a Great Place for Families".

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: To better support millennial families, we will adopt a three-pronged approach to encourage Singaporeans to form families and have children earlier.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: From the feedback gathered, we know that many Singaporeans would like to have their own homes before having children.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: Hence, our priority will be to help young couples who wish to settle down to get faster access to public housing.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: Second, as more women and grandparents are remaining in the workforce, some young parents are worried that they will not have anybody to care for their children when their maternity or paternity leave ends.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: Hence, the Government will increase the capacity and enhance the quality of centre-based infant care, so that parents will enjoy peace of mind when they return to work.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: Third, new parents would like better workplace and community support, so that they can manage both career and family commitments.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: Hence, we will work together with businesses and community organisations to better support millennial parents.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: Parents who need to send their child to centre-based care could then do so with greater peace of mind, when the child is older.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: However, it is not enough for the Government to act alone.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: We hope more employers can implement flexible work arrangements to enable employees to manage their career and family commitments.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: We also hope co-workers can show mutual understanding and support when their colleague needs to take time off work to care for their young child or elderly parent.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: There is an African idiom, "It takes a village to raise a child".

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: We need to mobilise the whole community and encourage more ground-up initiatives, such as parent support groups and family activities, so that millennials can be assured that parenthood is achievable, enjoyable and celebrated.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: (In English): To conclude, families are the foundation of society and our efforts to strengthen these foundations must never cease.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: Last year, I outlined our vision to make Singapore a Great Place for Families, where marriage and parenthood are achievable, enjoyable and celebrated.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: The enhancements will help couples get a place of their own sooner, have more peace of mind in the care for their infants and enjoy greater workplace and community support.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: We know it is not enough for the Government to act alone.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: Everyone − family, friends, employers, co-workers and the community − must come on board.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: Together, we can assure that millennials experience Singapore as a place where they can achieve their dreams, enjoy their families and careers, and celebrate their children with their communities.

speaker: The Chairman
text: Ms Sylvia Lim, you have two cuts, please take them together.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: The rationale for the TDSR policy is well-known.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: While the Government has a good intention, TDSR is a blunt instrument that has seriously affected certain groups of Singaporeans in the current economic climate.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: I raised this in a recent Parliamentary Question, but feel compelled to raise it again as some of our residents are in the affected group.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: The TDSR restricts borrowing from financial institutions to 60% of a person's monthly income, and applies not only to loans to purchase a property, but also to loans secured on a property.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: The first affected group will be retirees who have properties to mortgage but no income, who may need some liquidity for one reason or another.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: A second affected group would be those who have suffered a drop in income or been retrenched in the current downturn, but who can offer property as collateral for a loan.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: What these persons ask for is a tweak to the TDSR policy to give them flexibility to re-schedule their debt obligations, at little risk to the lenders.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: It seems that banks are applying TDSR strictly, with no or few exceptions.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: A Malaysian government investment company, 1Malaysia Development Berhad (1MDB) has spawned criminal and regulatory investigations into embezzlement or money laundering in at least 10 countries.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: Billions of funds associated with 1MDB and wealthy financier Jho Low have reportedly flowed through bank branches in Singapore.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: The repercussions on our banking industry have been severe.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: All these happened after last year's COS debates when Minister Chan Chun Sing said that MAS has put in place a "robust preventive regime".

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: However, even MAS has acknowledged that "it is not possible to prevent regulatory breaches and misconduct even with intrusive supervision".

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: Therefore, we are still very reliant on financial institutions and their employees themselves being vigilant and filing suspicious transaction reports.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: This regimen breaks down when institutions themselves have fostered a culture of non-compliance, as we have seen with BSI and Falcon Bank, in how they wilfully ignored the risks in the 1MDB-related transactions.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: Billions in transactions and millions in bonuses are tremendous incentives to break the law.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: Even with vigorous enforcement, punishments will only be meted out after the fact and Singapore's reputation in this regard will still be damaged.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Recently, some of our local banks were named for allegedly financing irresponsible palm oil companies linked to deforestation and the haze.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: In 2015, the Association of Banks in Singapore (ABS) released a set of industry guidelines to enhance responsible financing, but it seems that these measures have not borne fruit.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: International banks, such as HSBC, has started to strengthen their lending criteria, but local banks have not published environment, social and governance policies.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Will MAS encourage financiers to adhere to ABS' guidelines, and what further steps will it take to prevent local financiers' involvement in environmental disruption, which could lead to haze?

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Nee Soon)
text: Many public listed company executives tell me of the challenges of abiding by a growing checklist of regulations.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Nee Soon)
text: At the same time, there are rapid changes internationally with regard to compliance.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Nee Soon)
text: I note that MAS recently established the Corporate Governance Council to review the Code of Corporate Conduct.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Nee Soon)
text: How can we ensure that this code of conduct, while meeting international standards, will be practical and supportive of businesses, as well as to improve the attractiveness of our exchanges?

speaker: Ms Chia Yong Yong
text: Bona vacantia	properties and estates accrue to the Government, but there is a category of monies that may not be	bona vacantia.

speaker: Ms Chia Yong Yong
text: Rather, they could just simply be unclaimed by the owners and, these properties, monies, could be held in private or public institutions.

speaker: Ms Chia Yong Yong
text: Is there legislation for the Government to expropriate such monies?

speaker: The Minister for Education (Higher Education and Skills) and Second Minister for Defence (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: Retirees, who have fully paid up their properties, may want to take up a mortgage to support their children's education, pay medical fees, support retirement expenses and, maybe, start new companies.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Higher Education and Skills) and Second Minister for Defence (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: But some of them are unable to do so today under the TDSR rules.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Higher Education and Skills) and Second Minister for Defence (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: I do remember Ms Sylvia Lim asking this question last year.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Higher Education and Skills) and Second Minister for Defence (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: It is the same question, but I will give the same answer, which is, that MAS has been receiving similar feedback.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Higher Education and Skills) and Second Minister for Defence (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: Ms Sylvia Lim also asked about our anti-money laundering (AML) regime and the efficacy of related agencies and what steps we will take.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Higher Education and Skills) and Second Minister for Defence (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: Singapore is a global business and financial centre.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Higher Education and Skills) and Second Minister for Defence (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: It sees substantial financial flows daily, in many forms.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Higher Education and Skills) and Second Minister for Defence (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: Every such global centre carries risks relating to money laundering and other financial crimes.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Higher Education and Skills) and Second Minister for Defence (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: Increasingly, criminals are developing complex, cross-border schemes to mask illicit flows or ill-gotten gains through financial centres around the world.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Higher Education and Skills) and Second Minister for Defence (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: It is a clear example − it is, by far, one of the most complex, sophisticated and largest money laundering cases to date.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Higher Education and Skills) and Second Minister for Defence (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: These flows were channelled through multiple jurisdictions, including the US, Switzerland, Hong Kong, Luxembourg, the Netherlands, Barbados and through many parties and entities, of which many were shell companies incorporated in the British Virgin Islands, Cayman Islands and Seychelles.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Higher Education and Skills) and Second Minister for Defence (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: We have taken many steps and a robust approach to addressing these risks, because trust and rule of law underpin our international reputation.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Higher Education and Skills) and Second Minister for Defence (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: It is a moving game, and our approaches and methods have to keep evolving.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Higher Education and Skills) and Second Minister for Defence (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: First, we put in place a strong regulatory regime against money laundering, complemented by close supervision, unstinting enforcement where there are offences in Singapore and active international co-operation.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Higher Education and Skills) and Second Minister for Defence (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: Because of the severity and complexity of 1MBD, in fact, we started the Supervisory Examinations two years ago on banks that were suspected of being involved.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Higher Education and Skills) and Second Minister for Defence (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: The Financial Action Task Force, endearingly known as FATF, has independently assessed our system last year and re-affirmed Singapore's strong regulatory framework, alert supervision of the financial sector.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Higher Education and Skills) and Second Minister for Defence (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: Second, we have effective use of financial intelligence by the Suspicious Transaction Reporting Office.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Higher Education and Skills) and Second Minister for Defence (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: And also, we share intelligence with our counterparts all over the world.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Higher Education and Skills) and Second Minister for Defence (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: But as the 1MDB example shows, even with strong rules, we cannot eliminate financial crime.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Higher Education and Skills) and Second Minister for Defence (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: This is why we need deterrent enforcement, and that is our third step.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Higher Education and Skills) and Second Minister for Defence (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: And this has included senior management in some of these banks.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Higher Education and Skills) and Second Minister for Defence (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: We believe the message has gone out loud and clear − Singapore will not tolerate the criminal abuse of our financial system.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Higher Education and Skills) and Second Minister for Defence (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: Mr Louis Ng asked if MAS will encourage local financiers to adhere to the Association of Banks in Singapore (ABS) industry guidelines on responsible financing.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Higher Education and Skills) and Second Minister for Defence (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: MAS has been working closely with the financial industry on this.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Higher Education and Skills) and Second Minister for Defence (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: The local banks have established internal task forces on environment, social and governance issues to help integrate the ABS Guidelines into their lending and business practices.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Higher Education and Skills) and Second Minister for Defence (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: Banks have implemented environmental risk weightings as part of their loans assessment criteria.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Higher Education and Skills) and Second Minister for Defence (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: Loan decisions relating to companies which are assessed to have high environmental risks will be escalated to the banks' senior management.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Higher Education and Skills) and Second Minister for Defence (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: ABS has also recently introduced specific guidelines for banks on dealing with haze-related risks, such as no open burning on plantations, and build capacity on fire prevention with local communities.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Higher Education and Skills) and Second Minister for Defence (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: Mr Henry Kwek has raised a concern on increasing complexity in regulation and the rising cost of compliance, specifically in the area of corporate governance.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Higher Education and Skills) and Second Minister for Defence (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: As an international financial centre, we must ensure that our system remains sound and effective, and stays abreast of international norms.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Higher Education and Skills) and Second Minister for Defence (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: On corporate governance, ours is a tiered approach.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Higher Education and Skills) and Second Minister for Defence (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: The Companies Act sets out fundamental requirements for directors to act honestly and use reasonable diligence in discharging their duties.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Higher Education and Skills) and Second Minister for Defence (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: The Code of Corporate Governance sets out corporate governance best practices and applies to listed companies on a comply-or-explain basis.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Higher Education and Skills) and Second Minister for Defence (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: To ensure that our corporate governance regime remains progressive and relevant, MAS has formed a Corporate Governance Council to review the Corporate Governance Code and practices.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Higher Education and Skills) and Second Minister for Defence (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: The Council members are drawn from various stakeholder groups, including small medium enterprises (SMEs), to provide broad and diverse perspectives on Corporate Governance issues.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Higher Education and Skills) and Second Minister for Defence (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: Ms Chia Yong Yong asked if there is any legislation that empowers the Singapore Government to expropriate unclaimed funds held by non-Government entities, such as banks and other professional or commercial entities.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Higher Education and Skills) and Second Minister for Defence (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: Owners retain their legal right of claim even when their accounts have been inactive.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang
text: Allow me to seek some clarifications about our Public Service and also make some clarifications.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang
text: As I have mentioned in my speech, the issue is not only about our public servants but I think, more importantly, about the system they work in.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang
text: As I have mentioned, in our pursuit to automate most things, we now have a system without a heart.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang
text: So, in the example that I shared, the HDB officer had a heart and wanted to help the resident but the computer did not have a heart and the letter demanding payment was computer-generated.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang
text: That is the problem we need to tackle.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang
text: My speech was also drafted in consultation with the public servants who are on the ground and who are frustrated.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang
text: Hence, my first suggestion, which is from them, is that we need to cut some slack for our ground officers, our frontline staff members who will be the first to detect people who have fallen through the cracks, who can alert us.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang
text: Many I have spoken to feel that when they bring such cases to their superiors, they are scolded for not following the books.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang
text: We need to develop a culture where they are not being penalised for being different.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang
text: Can I ask the Deputy Prime Minister to clarify what steps we are taking to develop this culture?

speaker: Mr Teo Chee Hean
text: First of all, I would like to thank Mr Louis Ng for supporting our public officers in making his clarification.

speaker: Mr Teo Chee Hean
text: Of course, computers have no heart; public servants do.

speaker: Mr Teo Chee Hean
text: And I would encourage him to continue to encourage his officers who work so closely with him to serve his residents together with him.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang
text: I am thankful for our public servants and I do work closely with them.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang
text: As I have mentioned, they are a rare breed who devote their lives towards serving Singapore.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang
text: I just want to add a point, which is, as we cut budgets, I hope we can consider the impact this has on individual public servants.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang
text: I want to share a comment that was sent to me and I will read it out.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang
text: The quote is, "You think I do not want to go the extra mile for my country?

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang
text: I got heart but I got time boh?

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang
text: We always kena headcount freeze, or worse, headcount cut.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang
text: Keep telling me to exercise compassion and empathy.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang
text: Legislate more support for public officers first then we talk."

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang
text: The clarification is: as we cut budgets, can we consider the impact this has on the individual public servants?

speaker: Mr Teo Chee Hean
text: And I think, as a number of Members have pointed out, this is work that is not just for the public officers, and as I have said in my reply, every Member of this House, together with public officers, members of the public and VWOs, we all have a role to play, too.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera
text: I just want to thank Senior Minister of State Josephine Teo for her response.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera
text: I just want to seek a few clarifications regarding my cut on the new Singapore Citizenship Journey.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera
text: And lastly, if there is a doubt about the facts, would the Government not agree to conducting a study to ascertain if this is, indeed, something that not all new citizens fully understand?

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: Is it the Member's view or contention that citizens born in this country know that the vote is secret, but for some strange reason, our new citizens do not know that their vote is secret?

speaker: Mr Leon Perera
text: The Senior Minister of State may not be aware that I have, in fact, raised this as a Parliamentary Question (PQ) about born-in-Singapore citizens.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera
text: I raised it as a PQ to Minister Ng Chee Meng, I believe, and it was answered last year that this education gap could also be an issue for born-in-Singapore citizens.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera
text: I do not only have that concern for new citizens.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera
text: It is also a concern for born-in-Singapore citizens.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera
text: I asked if the school curriculum could educate students on that, and that was a PQ that is in the Hansard.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera
text: But my cut here is in the context of new citizens only.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera
text: So, that is what I am referring to in this particular instance.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera
text: But it is also an issue for born-in-Singapore citizens.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: So, may I confirm then that this issue has nothing to do with new citizens per se?

speaker: Mr Leon Perera
text: My cut is specifically asking about new citizens and the new citizen guidebook, and if there can be some education.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: But Mdm Chairman, the Member just said he also asked about the secrecy of votes and the knowledge of such amongst all citizens, not just new citizens.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: So, it has nothing to do with new citizens per se.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera
text: I was referring to my PQ last year in response to your clarification to my clarification.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera
text: You asked if I only have this concern about new citizens.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera
text: I do have this concern for born-in-Singapore citizens as well.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: As I have mentioned in my reply, the vast majority of all adult new citizens have lived in Singapore for at least five years before naturalisation, which means that they would have witnessed at least an electoral cycle, usually.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: When we are in an election, I do not think in all of the elections that I have taken part in as a voter has the issue of electoral fraud been prominent.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: The secrecy of the vote, I think, is something that I have learnt as a little girl, watching television, from young, come election time, there is a television advertisement that tells you, "Your Vote is Secret".

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: I have learnt that my entire life and I do not know of many other fellow citizens who would doubt that.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: I urge the Member not to be overly worried about this.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: If there is anyone that he comes across that has any further doubt on this, they can certainly visit our Elections Department's website and be reassured.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera
text: I appreciate what the Senior Minister of State has said.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera
text: I had, as I mentioned in my cut, actually met a number of new citizens who are not clear about this.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera
text: My clarification would be: what would be the problem or impediment to just including a write-up to educate new citizens about that in the guidebook?

speaker: Mr Leon Perera
text: What would be the issue in doing that?

speaker: Mr Teo Chee Hean
text: The ones who had been saying that the vote was not secret in the past was exactly the Workers' Party until you discovered it was not really such a good idea to say that your vote is not secret.

speaker: Mr Teo Chee Hean
text: And suddenly, you changed your mind and are now going out to tell people that your vote is secret, for which we are grateful.

speaker: Mr Teo Chee Hean
text: The Government has been saying that all along and we are glad that you agree.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim
text: So, my question is whether the Minister agrees that, actually, the Government or we are still on a learning curve on how to respond adequately to these, as he says, complex cross-border transactions.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: Having said that, I take Ms Sylvia Lim's point, this is always a learning process.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: In Chinese:道 高 一 尺，魔 高 一 丈.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: When the moral is one feet, the evil is 10 feet.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: We will constantly have to learn, work with our foreign counterparts, exchange intelligence, work together and tackle this.

speaker: Mr Low Thia Khiang
text: Would the Deputy Prime Minister clarify when the Workers' Party said the vote is not secret?

speaker: Mr Teo Chee Hean
text: I recall the Workers' Party has made an issue about registration numbers on voters' slips and so forth.

speaker: Mr Teo Chee Hean
text: Mr Low may choose not to remember, but those were issues which were raised before, I think even in this House.

speaker: Mr Yee Chia Hsing (Chua Chu Kang)
text: I am very happy to hear from Mr Ong Ye Kung that MAS is looking at unclaimed funds in bank accounts.

speaker: Mr Yee Chia Hsing (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Can I also ask him if they are also looking at unclaimed insurance policies?

speaker: Mr Yee Chia Hsing (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Because a lot of people buy insurance policies and when they die, the family members do not know what policies they have bought or from where.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: MAS, I am sure, will take a look at it.

speaker: The Chairman
text: Mr Cedric Foo, do you wish to withdraw your amendment?

text: I suspend the Sitting and will take the Chair again at 5.40 pm.
